response.text:
No direct controlled study emerged comparing title-lexical negatives against uniform negatives specifically for an item-ID-only sequential model trained with sampled cross-entropy. Related evidence supports distinguishing lexical similarity from model-score hardness. [On the Theories Behind Hard Negative Sampling (WWW 2023)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3543507.3583223) links score-based hard sampling under BPR to top-K ranking objectives and validates controllable hardness on three benchmarks; this does not establish that title overlap supplies useful hard negatives. [SRNS (NeurIPS 2020)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2020/hash/0c7119e3a6a2209da6a5b90e5b5b75bd-Abstract.html) finds false negatives tend to maintain stable predictions across training, motivating selection using both high scores and prediction variance. [UFNRec (SDM 2023)](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9781611977653.ch6) demonstrates sequential-recommendation gains from identifying and exploiting likely false negatives rather than simply penalizing them.

Popularity effects are also substantial: [Prakash et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.17276v2) compare six samplers using SASRec/BCE, three datasets and 20 repeats. Uniform sampling favors head items; popularity/in-batch sampling can improve balance while sacrificing aggregate accuracy. These findings concern different objectives/backbones, so transfer to BERT4Rec sampled cross-entropy remains uncertain. Inference for the proposed mechanism: title similarity may select informative competitors, plausible positives, or popularity-correlated items; existing evidence does not isolate which dominates. A discriminating experiment would compare uniform, lexical, popularity-matched random and model-score-hard negatives with equal negative counts and training budgets, measuring validation HR@10, negative-score distributions, title overlap and training-popularity strata. Gains over uniform alone would not establish improved semantic discrimination.
